\begin{abstract}
Leadership communication is widely assumed to move financial markets, and a growing literature reports directional accuracies of 74--87\% from NLP pipelines built on such text. We construct one such pipeline and test the assumption directly. Our corpus is 1{,}288 communications from May 2016 to August 2026 --- 746 Federal Reserve and 472 ECB documents alongside 70 Mann ki Baat broadcasts, so 94.6\% is central-bank rather than domestic political text --- aligned to daily prices for 16 instruments, giving 16{,}832 event observations. Evaluation uses a cross-sectional target whose baseline is exactly 50\% by construction, expanding-window walk-forward refits, and errors clustered across 484 event dates.

Rhetoric features score 49.99\%, 95\% interval $[49.94, 50.03]$. A sweep from 1 to 252 trading days holds rhetoric-only accuracy within 49.88--50.02\% at every lag, ruling out delayed transmission. Under the absolute-direction framing, fitted models trail a naive always-up rule by 5.86 percentage points, and Granger tests across ten topics yield zero discoveries surviving Benjamini--Hochberg correction. As a positive control the same pipeline predicts realized-volatility direction at 68.67\% ($+17.07$pp over baseline, $z=+23.75$): the harness detects structure where structure exists, and rhetoric adds nothing there either.

Two bounds qualify the null --- the corpus composition above, and FinBERT's 512-token limit, which exposes 10.7\% of a median transcript --- so we claim no \emph{detectable} signal under this design, not a general absence. Finally, tuning the horizon to 252 days reports 75.28\%, a headline-grade figure that is 3.58pp \emph{worse} than a constant rule on the same rows. We release the pipeline and verification harness.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
market efficiency, political communication, null result, topic modeling, FinBERT, Granger causality, false discovery rate, backtest overfitting, walk-forward validation, realized volatility, Indian equity markets
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%=========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%=========================================================================
Classical theory holds that asset prices reflect all publicly available information \cite{fama1970}, yet an extensive literature documents apparent deviations around political and policy events. Leadership communication --- speeches, press conferences, and broadcast addresses such as \textit{Mann ki Baat} --- is a natural candidate for a high-density information channel shaping expectations, sector rotation, and risk appetite. The Indian equity market is an attractive setting, subject both to domestic policy communication and to monetary signals from the Federal Reserve and ECB that propagate through capital-flow and currency channels.

A reasonable hypothesis follows: a pipeline that ingests this communication, resolves its topical content, scores its sentiment, and aligns it to market data should extract measurable directional predictability. We built that pipeline and tested that hypothesis. It does not survive.

We report the null as the primary finding for three reasons. First, it is established under a design whose baseline is exactly 50\%, so it cannot be attributed to equity drift, and it holds across every forecast horizon from one day to one year. Second, the accuracies commonly reported in this area --- 74\% \cite{jain2023}, 87\% \cite{biswal2022}, $R^2=0.9866$ \cite{bhandari2025} --- are difficult to reconcile with market efficiency, and we reproduce figures in exactly that band on our own data using choices that add no predictive content. Third, a null accompanied by a reproducible harness is more useful than an unreplicable positive.

To establish that the null reflects the data rather than a weak pipeline, we include a positive control: the same features and protocol predict realized-volatility direction at 68.67\%, $+17.07$pp over baseline at $z=+23.75$. The machinery detects structure when structure is present; what it does not detect is directional signal in the rhetoric features.

Two properties of the design bound that claim, and we state them up front. The corpus is 94.6\% central-bank communication --- 1{,}218 ECB and Federal Reserve documents against 70 Mann ki Baat broadcasts --- so what we test is predominantly institutional monetary communication, with the Indian political channel measured on thin data. And FinBERT's 512-token limit exposes only 10.7\% of a median Mann ki Baat transcript to the sentiment model. The correct reading is therefore \textit{no detectable directional signal under this design}, not a general claim that leadership communication is uninformative.

The distinction we press throughout is between \textit{accuracy} and \textit{skill}. An accuracy figure is uninterpretable without three companions: the baseline a trivial rule achieves on the same window, the coverage it is computed over, and the clustering used for inference. Omit any one and a null becomes indistinguishable from a strong result.

\textbf{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A negative result that is hard to dismiss as a weak
implementation.} We separate the question ``is there signal?'' from ``is
this pipeline any good?'' by pairing the rhetoric null with a positive
control on the same features, protocol and code. A harness that returns
chance on rhetoric while recovering a $+17$pp effect on realized volatility
is not failing to look.

\item \textbf{An evaluation design under which drift cannot masquerade as
skill.} Absolute-direction accuracy is confounded by equity drift, which
rises with horizon and makes tuned windows look progressively better. Posing
the question cross-sectionally --- does this instrument beat the median
instrument after this speech? --- pins the baseline at exactly 50\% by
construction, so any margin is skill by definition.

\item \textbf{Evidence that the null is a property of the signal, not of the
window.} A lag defence is the natural objection to a short-horizon null. We
test all lags from one day to one year and find rhetoric-only accuracy
immobile at chance throughout, which closes that defence empirically rather
than by assertion.

\item \textbf{A demonstration that routine evaluation choices, not
misconduct, produce this literature's headline numbers.} Four defensible-in-
isolation decisions yield 72.7--100\% on our own data with no added
predictive content --- most instructively a tuned horizon reporting 75.28\%
while being worse than a constant rule. We argue that an accuracy figure is
uninterpretable without a stated baseline, coverage, and clustering scheme,
and adopt that convention throughout.

\item \textbf{A released pipeline and verification harness}, in which every
numeric claim in this paper is regenerated by a single script.
\end{enumerate}

%=========================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:relwork}
%=========================================================================
This work sits at the intersection of four literatures: market efficiency
and event studies, central-bank communication, textual analysis in finance,
and the methodology of evaluating predictive claims. We review each, with
attention throughout to the evaluation protocol that produced a reported
result, since that is what our own contribution turns on.

\subsection{Market Efficiency and the Information-Arrival Premise}
The premise this paper tests is that scheduled leadership communication
carries tradable information. Fama's efficient-market framework
\cite{fama1970, fama1991} predicts that publicly and simultaneously released
information is impounded into prices faster than a daily-resolution strategy
can exploit. Grossman and Stiglitz \cite{grossman1980} qualify this: markets
cannot be perfectly efficient, or no one would be paid to gather
information, implying a small equilibrium return to costly analysis.
Malkiel \cite{malkiel2003} surveys the critiques, and Lo's adaptive-markets
view \cite{lo2004} allows efficiency to vary across regimes and horizons.
The relevant question for us is not whether markets are efficient in the
abstract, but whether a broadcast watched by millions and pre-announced
weeks ahead leaves exploitable residue at daily frequency. Our design tests
exactly that.

\subsection{Event Studies}
The event-study apparatus originates with Fama et al.\ \cite{fama1969} and
was placed on firm statistical footing by Brown and Warner \cite{brown1985},
who documented how test specification and return-generating assumptions
drive inference. MacKinlay \cite{mackinlay1997} and Campbell et al.\
\cite{campbell1997} give the standard treatments, including the abnormal-
return construction and the event-window conventions we follow. Two of
their cautions bear directly on our results: normal-return benchmarks must
be estimated from pre-event data only, and overlapping event windows induce
cross-sectional dependence that invalidates naive standard errors. We
encountered the first as a concrete defect --- the pipeline's original
abnormal-return field subtracted a full-sample mean and so embedded post-
event information (Section~\ref{sec:results}) --- and the second motivates
our clustering scheme.

For the Indian setting specifically, Srivastava and Mitra
\cite{srivastava2019} find significant abnormal returns on SENSEX and Nifty
50 around the Pulwama--Balakot crisis persisting roughly 11 days. Their
result motivated this project. We stress that a discrete, unanticipated
geopolitical shock and a decade of scheduled monthly broadcasts are
different objects, and our findings suggest the latter does not inherit the
predictability of the former.

\subsection{Central-Bank Communication}
Because 94.6\% of our corpus is ECB and Federal Reserve text, the
central-bank communication literature is the closest reference class for our
null. Blinder et al.\ \cite{blinder2008} survey the field and conclude that
communication moves markets, but the identification strategies that
establish this are informative for us: they overwhelmingly rely on
high-frequency windows around announcements rather than daily returns.
Kuttner \cite{kuttner2001} isolates the unexpected component of policy
changes using futures data; Gürkaynak et al.\ \cite{gurkaynak2005} decompose
announcement effects into a target and a path factor; Bernanke and Kuttner
\cite{bernanke2005} trace the equity response to policy surprises;
Nakamura and Steinsson \cite{nakamura2018} identify monetary non-neutrality
in tight intraday windows. Romer and Romer \cite{romer2004} construct a
narrative measure of policy shocks from internal documents.

Two features of this literature are decisive for interpreting our result.
First, it consistently prices the \textit{unexpected} component of a
communication rather than its content --- a distinction our topic-share and
sentiment features do not capture, and one we flag as a limitation. Second,
its effects are identified at intraday resolution; our daily design cannot
observe a within-session response. Hansen et al.\ \cite{hansen2018} and
Hansen and McMahon \cite{hansen2016} apply text analysis directly to FOMC
deliberation and communication, and are the closest methodological
antecedents to our pipeline.

\subsection{Textual Analysis in Finance}
Loughran and McDonald \cite{loughran2011} established that general-purpose
sentiment dictionaries systematically misclassify financial language, and
their later survey \cite{loughran2016} maps the field. Tetlock
\cite{tetlock2007} linked media pessimism to market returns, and Tetlock et
al.\ \cite{tetlock2008} showed that negative language in firm-specific news
forecasts earnings. Antweiler and Frank \cite{antweiler2004} analysed
message-board activity and found effects on volatility clearer than on
returns --- a pattern our own volatility control echoes. Garcia
\cite{garcia2013} shows sentiment effects concentrate in recessions;
Jegadeesh and Wu \cite{jegadeesh2013} refine term weighting for document
tone. Gentzkow et al.\ \cite{gentzkow2019} survey text-as-data methods
across economics, and Baker and Wurgler \cite{baker2006} provide the
investor-sentiment framing that motivates much of this work.

We note a recurring asymmetry across these studies: effects on second
moments are more robust than effects on first moments. Our results are
consistent with it, and we make the comparison explicit by measuring both.

\subsection{Language Models and Topic Models}
Transformer architectures \cite{vaswani2017} and BERT \cite{devlin2019}
underpin the sentence and document encoders now standard in this area.
Araci \cite{araci2019} further-pretrained BERT on financial corpora to
produce FinBERT, which we adopt; Paul et al.\ \cite{paul2024} report 89.6\%
accuracy for it on financial text classification. Reimers and Gurevych
\cite{reimers2019} introduced Sentence-BERT for efficient semantic
similarity. For Indian languages, Kakwani et al.\ \cite{kakwani2020} released
IndicBERT and the IndicNLP corpora, which would be the natural route to
processing Hindi-language Mann ki Baat audio transcripts --- a direction we
identify as future work rather than claim here.

On the topic side, Latent Dirichlet Allocation \cite{blei2003} and
non-negative matrix factorization \cite{lee1999} are the two standard
decompositions; Röder et al.\ \cite{roder2015} systematised the coherence
measures used to select among them, and Grootendorst \cite{grootendorst2022}
introduced BERTopic. Applications to finance include Buehlmaier and Whited
\cite{buehlmaier2018} on 8-K filings, Mishev et al.\ \cite{mishev2022} on
multi-label announcement classification, and Seng and Lim \cite{seng2023},
who report that BERTopic features improve downstream error metrics. We
implemented an LDA/NMF/BERTopic ensemble and removed it for reasons reported
in Section~\ref{sec:pipeline}.

\subsection{Machine Learning for Return Prediction}
LSTM networks \cite{hochreiter1997} dominate the applied literature: Fischer
and Krauss \cite{fischer2018} apply them to S\&P 500 constituents, and
Kumar et al.\ \cite{kumar2024} report 2.36\% error on ICICI Bank data.
Khadke et al.\ \cite{khadke2023} compare CNN and LSTM ($R^2$ of 0.922 versus
0.88); Chen et al.\ \cite{chen2024} model asymmetric lead--lag structure with
a relational temporal graph network, motivating our instrument-identity and
cross-sectional features. Bhandari et al.\ \cite{bhandari2025} combine a GRU
over prices with FinBERT and BERTopic news features, reporting
$R^2 = 0.9866$. Jain et al.\ \cite{jain2023} report over 74\% directional
accuracy from headline embeddings, Biswal et al.\ \cite{biswal2022} 87\% via
Grey Relational Analysis, Rambola et al.\ \cite{rambola2021} link
public-figure sentiment to abnormal returns, and Ruz et al.\ \cite{ruz2024}
predict volatility from social-media metadata.

Gu et al.\ \cite{gu2020} provide the methodological counterweight from
within asset pricing: a large comparison of ML methods under strictly
out-of-sample, expanding-window protocol, whose realised gains are far
smaller than the applied literature's headline figures. Nazari et al.\
\cite{nazari2025} issue the corresponding warning from inside the applied
literature, reporting that such models frequently fail to beat buy-and-hold.
Our Table~\ref{tab:horizon} corroborates this at every horizon tested.

\subsection{Volatility and Regimes}
Volatility clustering, established by Engle \cite{engle1982} and Bollerslev
\cite{bollerslev1986}, is the mechanism behind our positive control.
Andersen et al.\ \cite{andersen2003} formalised realized volatility from
high-frequency returns, and Corsi \cite{corsi2009} showed that a simple
heterogeneous autoregressive model of realized volatility is difficult to
beat. That an off-the-shelf classifier reaches 68.67\% on volatility
direction is therefore expected rather than novel; its role here is to
demonstrate that our harness detects real structure. Regime-switching models
follow Hamilton \cite{hamilton1989}, with parameters estimated by the
Baum--Welch algorithm \cite{baum1970}; Ang and Bekaert \cite{ang2002} apply
regime shifts to asset allocation.

\subsection{Political and Policy Uncertainty}
Baker et al.\ \cite{baker2016} construct the Economic Policy Uncertainty
index from newspaper text, the most widely used quantification of the
channel we study. Pástor and Veronesi \cite{pastor2013} model political
uncertainty as a priced risk factor. Białkowski et al.\
\cite{bialkowski2008} document elevated volatility around national
elections, and Santa-Clara and Valkanov \cite{santaclara2003} report the
presidential-cycle return puzzle. Collectively these establish that
political conditions affect risk premia and second moments; none of them
claims that routine, scheduled political speech predicts short-horizon
directional returns, which is the narrower proposition we test and reject.

\subsection{Inference, Multiplicity, and Backtest Overfitting}
Granger causality \cite{granger1969} is the standard test for temporal
precedence and the one our pipeline applies. Correct inference in panel
event settings requires attention to dependence: Newey and West
\cite{newey1987} for serial correlation, Petersen \cite{petersen2009} for
finance panels specifically, and Cameron et al.\ \cite{cameron2011} for
multiway clustering. Politis and Romano \cite{politis1994} provide the
stationary bootstrap used for dependent resampling.

On multiplicity, Benjamini and Hochberg \cite{benjamini1995} give the
false-discovery-rate procedure we apply to our Granger tests; Romano and
Wolf \cite{romano2005} extend stepwise control to data-snooping settings;
White \cite{white2000} introduced the reality-check bootstrap. Harvey et
al.\ \cite{harvey2016} argue that most published cross-sectional return
predictors are false discoveries once the multiplicity of tested factors is
accounted for, and propose a substantially raised significance threshold.
Bailey et al.\ \cite{bailey2014} formalise backtest overfitting, showing
that sufficient strategy search manufactures impressive in-sample
performance from noise; López de Prado \cite{lopezdeprado2018} develops the
practical countermeasures. Ioannidis \cite{ioannidis2005} makes the general
case across empirical science. Diebold and Mariano \cite{diebold1995}
supply the formal test for comparing predictive accuracy that a full
ablation study would use.

\subsection{Synthesis: Two Literatures That Do Not Cite Each Other}
Read together, the studies above fall into two groups that reach
incompatible conclusions and largely ignore one another. The applied
text-and-markets work \cite{bhandari2025, jain2023, biswal2022, seng2023,
rambola2021} reports directional accuracies of 74--87\% and $R^2$ up to
0.9866, while the methodological literature in asset pricing
\cite{white2000, harvey2016, bailey2014, gu2020, lopezdeprado2018} holds
that effects of that magnitude almost never survive multiplicity correction
and honest out-of-sample protocol. Both cannot be right about the same
markets.

Three specific gaps explain the divergence, and each maps to a design choice
in this paper. First, \textit{baselines are usually unreported}: none of the
applied studies we reviewed states what a constant or persistence rule
achieves on its own test window --- precisely the comparison that separates
Table~\ref{tab:horizon}'s 75.28\% from skill. Second, \textit{dependence is
usually unmodelled}: panel designs pairing many assets with shared events
generate correlated rows, and unclustered standard errors overstate
significance, by $2.68\times$ in our data. Third, \textit{multiplicity is
usually uncorrected}: our own Granger analysis yields one nominally
significant topic and zero after FDR adjustment, an inversion an uncorrected
reading would report as a finding.

Nazari et al.\ \cite{nazari2025} is the closest existing warning from inside
the applied literature. We supply the quantitative version of it, on data
where the answer is known --- because we also measured what a working signal
looks like on the same pipeline.

\section{Data and Pipeline}
\label{sec:pipeline}

%=========================================================================
Fig.~\ref{fig:methodology} summarizes the pipeline end to end. The
subsections below describe each stage; the two design bounds noted in the
figure --- corpus composition and sentiment truncation --- recur throughout
because they set the scope of what the results can establish.

\subsection{Terminology}
Three terms recur and are not interchangeable, so we fix them here.
\textit{Leadership communication} is the umbrella: any scheduled public
address by an office-holder. \textit{Central-bank communication} means the
ECB and Federal Reserve speeches and press releases that constitute 94.6\%
of our corpus. \textit{Domestic political communication} means the Mann ki
Baat broadcasts, 70 documents or 5.4\%. Where a result concerns the corpus
as a whole we say leadership communication; where the distinction matters
for interpretation --- as it does for every conclusion in this paper --- we
name the component explicitly.

\subsection{Corpus}
Table~\ref{tab:corpus} summarizes the data. The attrition from raw documents
to the unit of inference proceeds in five steps, each of which we state
because the effective sample is much smaller than the row count suggests:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{1{,}288} documents ingested (746 Fed, 472 ECB, 70 Mann ki Baat).
\item \textbf{1{,}071} carry a parseable date and can be aligned to markets;
      217 are dropped for missing or unparseable dates.
\item \textbf{1{,}052} survive joining sentiment and topic features and
      requiring a complete trailing market window at every horizon.
\item \textbf{16{,}832} (document, instrument) observations follow, since
      each document is paired with each of the 16 instruments, spanning
      798 distinct event dates.
\item \textbf{10{,}099} of those fall in walk-forward test blocks and are
      actually scored; they collapse to \textbf{484} event-date clusters,
      which is the unit all standard errors are computed over.
\end{enumerate}

The last step is the one that matters for inference. The nominal 10{,}099
predictions are not 10{,}099 independent observations, for the reason given
in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}.

Mann ki Baat coverage is 70 of 125 numbered episodes; episodes 22--75 and 102 are absent from our source and reported as missing rather than imputed. The pooled corpus is consequently 94.6\% central-bank text, which we treat as a limitation rather than a design choice.

\subsection{Text Processing}
Documents are lowercased and stripped of URLs and non-alphanumeric content, then processed with spaCy. A part-of-speech filter retains nouns, proper nouns, verbs, and adjectives, which are lemmatized; short tokens, stopwords, and a domain stopword list of rhetorical formulae are removed. A Devanagari detector routes Hindi-dominant documents to an indic-nlp path; in the assembled corpus all Mann ki Baat transcripts are English, so this path is exercised only incidentally.

Topics come from TF-IDF followed by Non-negative Matrix Factorization with $K=10$, factorizing the term-document matrix $\mathbf{M}$ into non-negative $\mathbf{W},\mathbf{H}$ with $\mathbf{M}\approx\mathbf{WH}$. We initially implemented an LDA/NMF/BERTopic ensemble with coherence-weighted averaging and removed it: on a corpus of order $10^3$ documents the UMAP--HDBSCAN stage produced unstable clusters with large noise assignments, and ensemble coherence did not exceed NMF alone. We record this negative architectural result because it runs against the prevailing assumption that ensembling helps.

FinBERT assigns each document probabilities over \{positive, negative, neutral\}; we retain all three plus a compound score. Its 512-token limit truncates every document, and the severity is easy to understate. Measured with the model's own tokenizer over 40 documents per source, the median Mann ki Baat transcript is 4{,}804 tokens, so FinBERT observes \textbf{10.7\%} of it; the figures are 17.6\% for ECB and 13.8\% for Fed. Our sentiment features describe each document's opening passage, not the document.

\subsection{Market Features}
A three-state Gaussian HMM fitted to index log-returns by Baum--Welch assigns each trading day a latent regime. Asset-specific baseline normalization expresses price as a trailing 252-day $z$-score. For each (document, instrument) pair we compute forward cumulative returns $r^{(n)}=\prod_{k=1}^{n}(1+r_{t+k})-1$ and forward realized volatility $\sigma^{(n)}=\mathrm{sd}(r_{t+1..t+n})$.

We target raw $r^{(n)}$ rather than the pipeline's abnormal-return field, which subtracts a \textit{full-sample} mean and therefore embeds post-event information. The magnitude effect is modest, but the analysis of interest is a sign test and the subtraction flips the sign of 4.6\% of events --- a caution that generalizes: a constant per-instrument offset is harmless for ranking and consequential for direction.

%=========================================================================
\section{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}
%=========================================================================
\textbf{Targets.} The \textit{absolute} target is $y=\mathbf{1}[r^{(n)}>0]$; its baseline is the majority class, which exceeds 50\% because equity returns drift upward. The \textit{cross-sectional} target is
\begin{equation}
y_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[r^{(n)}_{ij}>\operatorname{median}_j\!\left(r^{(n)}_{ij}\right)\right],
\label{eq:xs}
\end{equation}
asking whether instrument $j$ outperforms the median instrument following document $i$. Ties are dropped. This baseline is \textit{exactly} 50\% by construction, removing drift as a confound; our central claim rests on it. A third target, \textit{volatility direction} $\mathbf{1}[\sigma^{(n)}_{\text{fwd}}>\sigma^{(n)}_{\text{trailing}}]$, serves as a positive control.

\textbf{Features (196).} All computed strictly from pre-$t_i$ information: 5 sentiment, 10 topic probabilities, 160 topic$\times$instrument interactions, 16 instrument indicators, and 5 market controls (relative momentum over 5/10/20/60 observations and relative 20-day realized volatility), demeaned within each event as a relative target requires. The interactions encode the hypothesis under test.

\textbf{Validation.} Expanding-window walk-forward with five folds: fitted on all observations up to a fold boundary, predicting only the subsequent block, so no test observation informs any fit that predicts it. Models are $\ell_2$-regularized logistic regression at two penalty strengths and histogram gradient boosting, all from scikit-learn \cite{pedregosa2011} with fixed seeds, so repeated runs are bit-identical.

\textbf{Inference.} Each document contributes one observation per instrument, and those 16 rows share a single text and a single date. They are therefore not independent draws, and two distinct dependencies are at work: the instruments co-move (mean pairwise correlation of event-window returns $\rho=0.414$), and they share whatever idiosyncratic content that particular speech carried.

We cluster at the \textit{event date} rather than the document or the instrument. Clustering by instrument would be wrong in direction --- it treats the 16 co-moving series as the repeated unit when the shared shock is temporal. Clustering by document is nearly equivalent here, since documents rarely share a date, but event date additionally absorbs the case where two institutions speak on the same day and both events see the same market. Concretely, hit indicators are averaged within event date and the standard error is computed across the 484 resulting cluster means, so a date contributes once regardless of how many rows it generated. Section~\ref{sec:results} quantifies what ignoring this would cost: a design effect of 7.2, and standard errors understated by $2.68\times$.

%=========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
%=========================================================================
\subsection{Return Direction}
Table~\ref{tab:main} reports the central result. The strongest specification, gradient boosting, reaches 51.71\% against a 50\% baseline ($z=+2.90$) --- nominally significant across three specifications tested.

The ablation settles its interpretation. Restricting to rhetoric features alone --- sentiment and topic probabilities, the quantities this paper is about --- yields 49.99\% ($z=-0.63$), indistinguishable from chance, as do the topic$\times$instrument interactions in isolation (50.04\%). Market controls alone yield 50.63\%. The marginal edge is attributable to price momentum, not to leadership communication. On the hypothesis under test, the result is a clean null.

Under the absolute-direction target the picture is worse: an always-up rule achieves 56.46\%, gradient boosting 50.60\%, an edge of $-5.86$pp ($z=-6.00$). The fitted model is significantly worse than ignoring the data.

\subsection{Is There a Transmission Lag?}
A natural defence of the null is that rhetoric acts slowly, so a five-day window is simply too short. Table~\ref{tab:horizon} tests this directly across eight horizons.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Horizon sweep. ``Raw'' is absolute-target accuracy --- the figure a horizon-tuned claim would report; ``base'' is the always-up rule on the same window. Rhetoric-only uses the cross-sectional target (baseline exactly 50\%).}
\label{tab:horizon}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{rccrcr}
\toprule
\textbf{$h$} & \textbf{Raw} & \textbf{Base} & \textbf{Edge} & \textbf{Rhet.\ only} & \textbf{$z$} \\
\midrule
1 & 52.20\% & 52.33\% & $-0.14$ & 50.02\% & $+0.54$ \\
5 & 55.12\% & 56.41\% & $-1.29$ & 49.99\% & $-0.63$ \\
10 & 57.46\% & 59.25\% & $-1.80$ & 50.00\% & $+0.16$ \\
20 & 58.30\% & 60.21\% & $-1.91$ & 49.98\% & $-0.76$ \\
30 & 59.00\% & 60.85\% & $-1.85$ & 49.99\% & $-0.33$ \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Two findings. First, rhetoric-only accuracy is confined to 49.88--50.02\% at \textit{every} horizon; there is no lag at which leadership communication predicts relative returns, so the slow-transmission defence fails on its own terms.

Second, and central to Section~\ref{sec:inflate}: raw accuracy rises monotonically with horizon, reaching 75.28\% at one year --- a figure that would comfortably headline a paper. On the same window a constant ``up'' call scores 78.85\%. The model is 3.58pp \textit{worse} than doing nothing, at $z=-3.91$. Fig.~\ref{fig:horizon} shows the two curves; the visible gap between them is negative throughout.

\subsection{Positive Control: Volatility}
If the pipeline were simply weak, it would fail everywhere. Table~\ref{tab:vol} shows it does not: the same features and protocol predict realized-volatility direction far above baseline.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Volatility direction (will realized volatility rise or fall?). The pipeline works --- but rhetoric contributes nothing, and neither does India VIX. Increments are paired over date clusters.}
\label{tab:vol}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{$h$} & \textbf{Features} & \textbf{Hit} & \textbf{Edge vs base} \\
\midrule
\multirow{1}{*}{10d}
 & Market only & 68.67\% & $+17.07$pp ($z=+23.75$) \\
 & Rhetoric only & 50.82\% & $-0.79$pp \\
 & \textit{rhetoric increment} & \multicolumn{2}{l}{$-0.62$pp, $p=0.17$} \\

Volatility direction is predicted at 68.67\% against a 51.60\% baseline, an edge of $+17.07$pp at $z=+23.75$. This is volatility clustering, a well-established property of return series, and it establishes that our walk-forward harness detects real structure when real structure exists.

Rhetoric adds nothing to it. Incremental contributions across the three horizons are $-0.62$, $+0.61$, and $-0.11$ percentage points ($p=0.17$, $0.19$, $0.81$) --- inconsistent in sign and individually insignificant. India VIX, a direct forward-looking volatility measure previously unused in the pipeline, adds $+0.07$, $-0.04$, and $+0.33$pp ($p=0.90$, $0.94$, $0.55$). The second-moment channel, which we had considered the most plausible remaining route for a communication effect, is also null.

\subsection{Granger Causality with FDR Control}
Table~\ref{tab:granger} tests whether topic intensity Granger-causes market returns, taking the minimum F-test $p$-value over lags 1--5.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Granger causality, topic intensity $\rightarrow$ returns. Raw $p$ is the minimum over lags 1--5; $q$ is the Benjamini--Hochberg adjustment across ten topics.}
\label{tab:granger}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Topic} & \textbf{Raw $p$} & \textbf{BH $q$} \\
\midrule
Respondent, Quintile, SPF & 0.0100 & 0.100 \\
Financial Stability \& Markets & 0.0539 & 0.183 \\
Labor, Inflation, Percent & 0.0550 & 0.183 \\
ECB, European, Medium Query & 0.1622 & 0.406 \\
Payment, Digital, Stablecoin & 0.3096 & 0.521 \\
Term Condition, Net, Survey Round & 0.3124 & 0.521 \\
Village, Life, Youth & 0.4026 & 0.575 \\
Monetary Policy \& Inflation & 0.4604 & 0.576 \\
National Unity \& Commemoration & 0.6233 & 0.693 \\
Euro Area, Euro, ECB & 0.7501 & 0.750 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textbf{Discoveries at $q<0.05$: 0 of 10}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

No topic survives correction. More instructive: taking a minimum across five lags is itself a selection procedure. Under the null, $P(\min_{1..5}p<0.05)=1-0.95^5=0.226$, so across ten topics the expected number of nominal hits is 2.26. We observe one. The raw count is \textit{below} chance expectation, and an uncorrected reading --- which would report one significant topic --- inverts the actual inference. The sole nominal hit loads on \textit{respondent}, \textit{quintile}, and \textit{SPF}: vocabulary from the ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters, describing survey instrumentation rather than economic rhetoric.

\subsection{How Evaluation Design Manufactures Accuracy}
\label{sec:inflate}
Table~\ref{tab:inflate} applies four routine choices to this same data. Each yields a figure in the band this literature reports; none adds predictive skill.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Accuracy obtainable on this dataset without predictive skill. All
four are evaluated on the walk-forward test rows of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}
unless the third column says otherwise, so they are directly comparable to
Table~\ref{tab:main}. The first row breaks nothing at all --- it is the
protocol run honestly at a tuned horizon, which is what makes it the most
instructive of the four.}
\label{tab:inflate}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{2.2cm}cp{1.9cm}p{2.0cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Choice} & \textbf{Reported} & \textbf{Protocol element broken} & \textbf{What it actually is} \\
\midrule
Horizon $\rightarrow$ 252 days & 75.28\% & none --- the protocol is intact & Baseline on the \textit{same} rows is 78.85\%; the model is 3.58pp \textit{worse} \\
Random forest, in-sample & 100.0\% & no train/test split & Memorization of 16{,}832 rows \\
Post-event variable added & 72.7\% & feature causality & Target algebraically inside the features \\
Top 1\% most-confident & 78.0\% \textit{or} 50.0\% & full-coverage reporting & $n=50$; flips sign with target choice \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The horizon effect deserves emphasis as the least obviously improper, and Table~\ref{tab:horizon} shows why: a researcher who tunes the window to maximize reported accuracy lands at 252 days and 75.28\%, which is both an attractive number and 3.58pp worse than a constant rule.

The selective-reporting case is subtler, since restricting to high-confidence predictions is defensible as selective prediction. The defence fails on two grounds. First, the coverage curve (Fig.~\ref{fig:coverage}) is non-monotonic --- 51.2\%, 50.6\%, 49.3\%, 49.8\%, 50.7\%, 51.7\% as coverage falls from 100\% to 2\% --- whereas genuine confidence calibration produces a monotone increase. Second, and decisively, the same top-1\% procedure with identical features and split yields 78.0\% under the absolute target and 50.0\% under the cross-sectional target. A statistic whose value depends on the target definition at $n=50$ is noise.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figs/fig_coverage.png}
\caption{Hit rate against retained coverage, with 95\% intervals from date-clustered standard errors. Calibrated confidence would rise monotonically as coverage falls; this curve wanders within its intervals.}
\label{fig:coverage}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Pseudo-Replication}
Each document generates one record per instrument, and the instruments co-move strongly: mean pairwise correlation of event-window returns is $\rho=0.414$ across $k=16$ instruments. The design effect is
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{deff}=1+(k-1)\rho=1+15(0.414)=7.2,
\label{eq:deff}
\end{equation}
so an apparent 10{,}099 records carry the information of roughly 1{,}400, and unclustered standard errors are understated by $\sqrt{7.2}=2.68\times$. Reported significance that does not state its clustering scheme is uninterpretable in this setting.

%=========================================================================
\section{Discussion}
%=========================================================================
The most economical explanation is the standard one. Mann ki Baat is a pre-announced, nationally broadcast monthly address; ECB and Fed communications are scheduled and intensely scrutinized. Any information content reaches all participants simultaneously at zero cost, and weak-form efficiency \cite{fama1970} predicts incorporation faster than a daily-resolution pipeline can act on.

Three pieces of evidence make this hard to attribute to a weak implementation. The ablation shows rhetoric at exactly chance while momentum controls carry the entire marginal effect. The horizon sweep shows the same at every lag from one day to one year, closing off delayed transmission. And the volatility control shows the identical harness detecting a $+17$pp effect where genuine structure exists. A pipeline that finds volatility clustering at $z=+23.75$ and rhetoric at $z=-0.63$ is not failing to look.

This does not establish that leadership communication is irrelevant to markets. It establishes something narrower: at daily resolution, over a decade of routine communications, using topic distributions and document-level sentiment, there is no directional edge to extract, in first or second moments. The event-study finding of \cite{srivastava2019} around a discrete geopolitical shock is not contradicted.

Our second contribution follows from the first. Having found no signal, we could ask what it would take to \textit{appear} to find one, and the answer is: very little. When a study reports 74\% \cite{jain2023} or 87\% \cite{biswal2022} without stating the baseline a constant rule achieves on the same window, the coverage, and the clustering, a reader cannot distinguish a genuine edge from any of the mechanisms in Table~\ref{tab:inflate}. This is not an accusation about any particular paper; it is a statement about what the reported quantity identifies. The remedy is inexpensive: report baseline, coverage, and clustering alongside every accuracy figure. Our findings align with \cite{harvey2016} and \cite{bailey2014} on multiplicity and backtest overfitting; our Granger analysis is a small instance, where the uncorrected reading yields a publishable sentence and the corrected reading yields zero discoveries.

%=========================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
%=========================================================================
\textbf{Corpus composition.} Mann ki Baat coverage is 70 of 125 episodes with a contiguous gap (22--75), and the pooled corpus is 94.6\% central-bank text. The domestic channel is measured on thin data.
\textbf{Sentiment truncation.} FinBERT observes 10.7\% of a median Mann ki Baat transcript (17.6\% ECB, 13.8\% Fed). This is the limitation most likely to matter: our sentiment features characterize opening passages, and a chunk-and-aggregate scheme --- roughly 9$\times$ the compute at these lengths --- was not run. We cannot exclude that full-document sentiment carries signal this measure misses, and we would prioritize it over any other extension.
\textbf{Daily resolution.} Intraday incorporation is invisible to this design; a same-session effect would not appear in our data at all.
\textbf{Single regime era.} The 2016--2026 sample includes COVID-19 and an extended bull phase.
\textbf{Topic granularity.} Ten topics over a mixed-institution corpus is coarse.
\textbf{LLM attribution not evaluated.} A Groq-based company-attribution module is implemented and produces validated output, but corpus-wide coverage was not generated for this analysis and it contributes to no result reported here.

%=========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
%=========================================================================
We built an end-to-end pipeline linking political and central-bank communication to Indian equity markets and used it to test whether such communication carries exploitable directional signal. Across 1{,}288 documents, 16 instruments, two targets, three model classes, and eight forecast horizons, with walk-forward validation and date-clustered inference, it does not. Rhetoric features score 49.99\% against a 50\% baseline and remain within 0.2pp of 50\% at every horizon from one day to one year. Under the absolute target, fitted models underperform a naive rule by 5.86 points. Granger tests yield zero discoveries surviving FDR correction against a null expectation of 2.26 nominal hits. The same pipeline predicts volatility direction at 68.67\% ($z=+23.75$), establishing that the null reflects the signal rather than the method --- and rhetoric adds nothing there either.

We additionally quantify how readily this conclusion could have been reversed by evaluation choices rather than evidence. Tuning the forecast window to maximize reported accuracy yields 75.28\% at a 252-day horizon, a publishable-looking figure that is 3.58 points worse than a constant rule. In-sample fitting yields 100\%, one post-event variable yields 72.7\%, and a selectively-reported tail yields 78.0\% or 50.0\% depending on target. Unclustered inference overstates significance by 2.68$\times$. We conclude that accuracy figures in this literature require an accompanying baseline, coverage, and clustering scheme to be interpretable, and we release the pipeline and harness so these checks are cheap to apply.

Future work should pursue intraday alignment, since a same-session effect is the one channel this design cannot observe; complete full-document sentiment scoring; and replicate the harness on other emerging markets to test whether the null is India-specific or general to scheduled political communication.
